column1: What was the last film you saw and your conclusion was "This is the worst acting I have ever seen"? I walked out of the cinema fuming after watching *The Wretched* (2020). It’s a horror about a young teenager who discovers that his next-door neighbor is a witch who eats children. While this sounded intriguing in theory, the execution was terrible. The acting was so awful it was almost impressive. The main character, Ben, played by John-Paul Howard, was about as charismatic as week old bread. He had this perpetually constipated look on his face, like he was trying to remember where he parked his car. The other actors were just as bad. Specifically, the actor playing Abbie and her stepdad, whose names I can’t seem to remember. They each possessed no nuance in delivering their lines, sounding hollow and lifeless as if they’d been told to read from a script without any context or emotions. The supporting cast, unfortunately, brought nothing to elevate the film and it felt like a community theatre production gone terribly wrong. The dialogue sounded like it was written by a seventh grader, with no sense of realism. I mean, some of the lines were so clichéd and contrived that I almost laughed out loud, which is certainly not the reaction you want when watching a horror. The film was so bad that it lost me as an audience member and, surprisingly, the film was still scary. The witch herself was legitimately horrifying, but the bad acting made me want to switch it off. I gave it a 2/10. Avoid at all costs.

What does a $1,500,000 house look like where you live? Let me offer a glimpse into the landscape of the affluent in Trinidad and Tobago, where a $1.5 million house can buy you a substantial slice of paradise, though it's a very small slice in most cases. Forget gated communities and mansions, we are a small island and such properties are rare. The most likely scenario for something in this price range would be a large, well-appointed home, probably in a high-end suburban location.  Picture this: sprawling over an acre or two, a modern or colonial-style house boasting at least four spacious bedrooms, each with its own en-suite bathroom and walk-in closet. The design would likely feature an open-concept living area, seamlessly connecting a gourmet kitchen with top-of-the-line appliances to a living room that flows onto a covered patio. Outside, you'd find a generous, well-manicured lawn, possibly a private swimming pool, and maybe even a guest house or a staff quarters. The architecture could range from Mediterranean-inspired villas to contemporary designs, but what they have in common is a degree of artistry by professional landscape artists, interior designers and architects. Expect high-end finishes, from imported marble flooring to custom-built cabinetry and smart home technology, because the most expensive houses are at the beck and call of every whim of the affluent. Security, of course, would be paramount, with 24/7 monitoring, alarm systems, and maybe even an on-site security guard.  It will still be small though; the Caribbean is not the United States where one can buy acreage and a sprawling estate for this price. In any event, you are buying prime real estate and a lifestyle. You're paying for the views, the privacy, the convenience of location, and the prestige that comes with living in a sought-after address. In the world of affluence there are very small compromises.

Have you ever sabotaged food because someone was stealing it? Being a child of the 90s in Trinidad & Tobago, I grew up in a household where there were several children residing at all times. Whether it was my blood siblings or other relatives, they’d be at the house for weeks or months on end. As a result, we had to scrimp and save on everything to keep everyone fed, clothed and sheltered. This bred a war over food, with certain individuals having no regard for the careful rationing that was taking place. We had to be secretive. We had to be sneaky. To this day I can still picture my little sister devouring an entire batch of freshly baked cookies in one sitting.  My response: The culprits of the food theft were various, however the most brazen were close family members. They’d act as if the world was coming to an end if they didn’t get a bite to eat every few minutes. As soon as a meal or snack was prepared, it would vanish in a flash. The constant pilfering led me to resort to measures I'm not proud of now. I would often lace the food with substances that would make it unpalatable. For instance, I put a large amount of red pepper into a fruitcake, leading to one of my cousins literally spitting it out across the room. On another occasion, I put a liberal amount of dish soap into a large container of ice cream. Oh, how I cackled with glee as I saw the culprit’s incredulous face at the discovery of the sabotaged dessert. I knew I was being petty but the constant food thievery was a constant concern.

What was your cringiest moment with a boss? Several years ago, during my tenure at a particularly stifling IT firm, I found myself in a situation that still induces a palpable wave of mortification. It centered around a mandatory team-building exercise that was, to put it gently, a spectacular misfire. We were herded like cattle into a dimly lit conference room, the air thick with the aroma of stale coffee and forced camaraderie. The facilitator, a man whose enthusiasm seemed inversely proportional to his charisma, introduced the concept of trust falls. Yes, those relics of motivational seminars where you voluntarily hurl yourself backward into the dubious embrace of your colleagues. My boss, a man whose leadership style was rooted in intimidation and whose personality could chill the most seasoned individual wasn't a man to take part, and he decided to pass on participating in the fall. Now, I've always possessed a healthy skepticism for such manufactured displays of unity. Nonetheless, I was expected to engage. I stood with my colleagues, a knot of trepidation forming in my stomach. As my colleagues went ahead and went on to make the leap of faith. The air was thick with the stench of aftershave and fear. Then, it was my turn. With a deep breath, I stepped up to the ledge and prepared myself to take the plunge, when my boss, for reasons known only to himself, let out a bellow laugh.

Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? As a single man with no immediate plans to have children, I am often asked this question. It is sometimes followed by a well-intentioned jab: "You're getting old, you know!" or the more ominous, "You will regret it!" To be honest, I don’t see myself experiencing such intense feelings of deep regret. I don't think I’m going to have a moment in my old age where I clutch my chest, look at the bleakness of my barren apartment and dramatically exclaim, "Why didn't I have children?" This type of emotional outburst seems a bit theatrical to me. When some colleagues and family members offer parental advice, my reaction is sometimes a bored stare, or a polite nod, or a quick escape to the other side of the room. Most of the time, I am just mildly indifferent. All the same, I did have a few moments in my adult life where a part of me pondered the idea of having a child. These moments can be divided into three categories: the moments of societal pressure, the moments of personal reflection, and the moments of genuine love.
